# Authentication

> Send a bearer token in the Authorization header of every request to authenticate with the Tape API.

Send a bearer token in the `Authorization` header of every request to authenticate with the Tape API.

Tape accepts three kinds of bearer token for your own code. They differ in who obtains them and how much they may do. A fourth kind, the [automation API key](#automation-api-key), exists only inside automation runs.

## Usage example

**cURL**

```shell
curl https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/record/1 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TAPE_TOKEN"
```

**HTTP**

```http
GET /v1/record/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.tapeapp.com
Authorization: Bearer tape_pat_0a1b2c3d...
```

`$TAPE_TOKEN` holds your personal access token from the [Quickstart](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/guide/api/getting-started#step-1-create-a-personal-access-token). `1` is a record ID.

An OAuth access token goes in the same header. So does a user API key in existing integrations:

```shell
curl https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/record/1 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer tape_oat_0a1b2c3d..."
```

## Which credential to use

| You are… | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A developer calling the API directly: a script, an internal tool, an integration you build and run, including one that works in Tape on a user's behalf | A personal access token |
| Connecting an AI assistant or another MCP client to Tape | OAuth: the client [signs in with Tape](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/mcp/connect) |
| Building an integration or partner product that Tape registers, with a "Connect to Tape" or "Sign in with Tape" button | OAuth, with a [client registered by Tape](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/clients#a-client-registered-by-tape) |
| Maintaining an integration built on a user API key | Keep it running, and move it to a personal access token when you next work on it |

**Personal access tokens are the default.** Use one whenever you write code that calls the Tape API. A personal access token:

-   needs no client registration, no redirect and no consent screen
-   never needs refreshing
-   can be limited to the capabilities, workspaces and apps your code needs
-   can be revoked on its own without affecting anything else

The user your integration should act as creates the token and hands it to your integration.

Coming from the Podio API? Instead of app authentication, use a [personal access token limited to that app](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/guide/api/coming-from-podio#switch-authentication).

**OAuth is for MCP clients and registered integrations.** With OAuth, a person connects an app by signing in to Tape, without handling a secret. MCP clients use it to connect to the [Tape MCP server](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/mcp/overview). Integrations and partners registered by Tape use it for their sign-in. Building such an integration? [Ask Tape to register a client](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/clients#a-client-registered-by-tape).

## Comparing the credentials

|  | Personal access token | OAuth access token | User API key |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Used by | Developers calling the API directly | MCP clients, and integrations registered by Tape | Existing integrations |
| Prefix | `tape_pat_` | `tape_oat_` | `user_key_` |
| Obtained by | Creating it in your Tape settings | The user approving your app on Tape's consent screen | Copying it from your Tape settings |
| What it may do | Only the capabilities you grant it | Only the capabilities the user approved | Everything your user account can do |
| What it may reach | All, or only the workspaces and apps you select | Everything the user can reach | Everything you can reach |
| Lifetime | Until revoked | Access tokens last one hour and are renewed with a refresh token; the connection ends after 90 days unused, and for most apps a year after approval | Until deleted |
| Revoking | Individually, at any time | By the user, an organization admin, or the app | Only by deleting the single key |
| Status | Recommended | For MCP clients and registered integrations | Deprecated, existing integrations only |

> User API keys are deprecated
> 
> Existing user API keys keep working, but you can't limit them to capabilities, workspaces or apps. Deleting a key breaks every integration that uses it. Build new integrations on a personal access token.

## User API key

Each Tape user has one user API key. It acts as a bearer token for the API.

> Where do you find the user API key?
> 
> 1.  Select your profile picture, then select **Preferences**.
> 2.  In the settings window, select **Developer** (under **Features**).
> 3.  If you still have a user API key, it appears as **API Key** in the table of personal access tokens.
> 4.  Open its **⋯** menu and select **Copy API key** or **Delete**.

![Developer page in the settings window, selected under Features, with the table of personal access tokens and the New token button](https://developers.tapeapp.com/assets/images/developer-settings-00d5c9b8a127339f7ba33d92ce84f86a.png)

> Keep your user API key secret
> 
> Your user API key has the same privileges as your user account. If it leaks, delete it in the settings window under **Developer** and create a personal access token instead. A deleted key can't be restored.

## Personal access token

A personal access token is a named credential you create for one integration. You choose what it may do, and which workspaces and apps it may reach. Tokens start with `tape_pat_`, and Tape shows each one only once, when you create it.

-   [Personal access tokens](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/personal-access-tokens): create, limit and revoke a token.
-   [Capabilities](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/capabilities): the full list of what you can grant a token.

## OAuth access token

An app receives an OAuth access token when a Tape user connects it to their account:

1.  The app sends the user to Tape.
2.  The user approves the scopes the app asked for.
3.  The app gets an access token that acts as that user.

Tokens start with `tape_oat_`, last one hour, and are renewed with a refresh token. [OAuth](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/overview) describes the whole flow.

## Automation API key

An automation API key authenticates an automation, not a person. Tape creates a new one for each automation run. Keys start with `workflow_key_` and expire after a short time.

The `tape` client in an [**Execute a script** action](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/automations/introduction#tape-api-client) uses it, so your script doesn't handle authentication. You can't create, copy or revoke an automation API key yourself.

The key has no user behind it, so endpoints that need a user reject it, mostly with `400` or `401`. Where it works, Tape checks the automation's own access to the app or record. It works for:

-   the [discovery endpoints](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/automation/discovery) of the automation API
-   [calling an automation and generating a weblink](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/automation/advanced)
-   [listing the views of an app](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/app#retrieve-views-for-an-app)
-   [retrieving a single app](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/app#retrieve-a-single-app)
-   the record endpoints the built-in actions call: retrieve, create, update, delete and restore a record, filter records, retrieve the records of a view, record references and their statistics
-   [batch creating](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/record#batch-create-multiple-records) and [batch updating](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/record#batch-update-multiple-records) records
-   all [record revision endpoints](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/record-revision)
-   [unfollowing all records in a database app](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/record-follow)
-   creating a comment or a reply, and [deleting a comment or reply](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/record-comment#delete-a-comment-or-reply)
-   generating a PDF, sending an email and making an authenticated HTTP call
-   uploading files and creating a signed upload URL
-   the [automation usage report](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/automation-usage-report)

It doesn't work for managing apps, fields and views, retrieving a view, retrieving shared records, finding relatable records, updating record permissions, reading or listing comments and replies, deleting a comment with `DELETE /v1/comment/{comment_id}`, managing automations, listing automation runs, search, webhooks, users, workspaces and organizations.

Requests with an automation API key count against the run's own budget, not a user's. The `X-RateLimit-Scope` header shows `workflow`. See [Request limits](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/request-limits).

## Attribution

Every credential belongs to a user. Changes made with it show that user as the author, for example in the record's activity. You also don't get notifications for your own changes on records you follow.

To show an integration under its own name, create a dedicated user, for example "API User", and create the credential from that account.

## Authentication errors

Failed authentication with a personal access token or a user API key returns one of these responses. An OAuth access token that's no longer valid gets its own response. See [General behavior](#general-behavior).

*Invalid or unusable credential*

```json
{
  "status_code": 400,
  "endpoint": "/v1/record/1",
  "error_code": "validation",
  "error_message": "Invalid API key for accessing endpoint '/v1/record/1' (no active user for the given API key)"
}
```

*Malformed credential*

```json
{
  "status_code": 400,
  "endpoint": "/v1/record/1",
  "error_code": "validation",
  "error_message": "Invalid API key for accessing endpoint '/v1/record/1' (signature check not passed, key is malformed)"
}
```

*Missing credential*

```json
{
  "status_code": 401,
  "endpoint": "/v1/record/1",
  "error_code": "dev_api_authentication",
  "error_message": "Missing authentication for Dev-API endpoint: '/v1/record/1' (no user API key provided)"
}
```

The missing authentication response also carries `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://api.tapeapp.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/v1"`. An OAuth client finds Tape's authorization server there.

> Why do several causes return the same message?
> 
> An unknown token, a revoked token and a token whose owner was deactivated all return the same "no active user for the given API key" message. This is deliberate: different messages would let an unauthenticated caller probe which tokens exist.

**Getting an error?**

**Authentication error**

Check that you send the whole token, prefix included, after `Bearer` . If the token was revoked or lost, create a new one under **Developer**.

### General behavior

-   An OAuth access token that's no longer valid (expired, revoked or disconnected) returns `401` with the error code `dev_api_invalid_access_token`. The response carries a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"` header, whose `resource_metadata` points to the Developer API's protected resource metadata. See [Errors at the Developer API](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/authorization-flow#at-the-developer-api).
-   A personal access token or OAuth access token that authenticates but lacks the capability an endpoint requires returns `403`. See [Insufficient capabilities](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/capabilities#insufficient-capabilities).

# Capabilities and scopes

> The 17 capabilities a personal access token or an OAuth access token can hold, how they are requested, and how Tape enforces them.

Grant a credential only the capabilities it needs.

A *capability* is one thing a credential may do, such as reading records or sending email. Two kinds of credential carry capabilities, and Tape checks every request they make against them:

| Credential | Who decides its capabilities | When they are set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Personal access token](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/personal-access-tokens) | You, when you create the token | At creation, and never change |
| [OAuth access token](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/overview) | The app requests them; the user approves or declines on Tape's consent screen | At approval, and never widen |

A [user API key](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/authentication#user-api-key) carries no capabilities, and Tape never checks it against them.

> Capabilities or scopes?
> 
> Tape's settings call them *capabilities*, and the consent screen lists them as what an app can do. In the protocol they're called *scopes*: in OAuth's `scope` parameter, in token responses and in error messages. Scopes use the form `resource:action`, for example `records:read`.

## Capabilities only ever subtract

A credential acts as the user it belongs to. Its effective access is that user's own permissions, narrowed by its capabilities:

| Axis | Question it answers | Personal access token | OAuth access token |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **The user's own role** | What may this person do anyway? | Applies | Applies |
| **Capabilities** | What kind of action? | Chosen at creation | Approved at consent |
| **Content access** | Which workspaces and apps? | All, or only the ones you [select](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/personal-access-tokens#content-selection) | Everything the user can reach |

A capability never gives a credential access to something its user can't reach. When the user loses access to a workspace, every credential they own loses it too.

## The capabilities

| Area | Capability | Scope | What it allows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Organization** | Read organization | `organization:read` | View your organization and its members, including their names, email addresses and phone numbers. |
|  | Manage members | `organization.members:manage` | Invite people to your organization and manage invitations. Invitations can take up paid seats. |
| **Workspaces** | Read workspaces | `workspaces:read` | View workspaces and their members. |
|  | Edit workspaces | `workspaces:edit` | Create, rename and delete workspaces. Deleting a workspace also deletes the apps and records inside it. |
|  | Manage members | `workspaces.members:manage` | Add and remove workspace members. This gives other people access. |
| **Apps** | Read apps | `apps:read` | View apps together with their fields, views and settings. Also search across them. |
|  | Edit apps | `apps:edit` | Create, edit and delete apps, fields and views. Deleting a field also deletes its values in every record, and they cannot be restored. |
| **Records** | Read records | `records:read` | View records, their field values, files and full revision history, including values that were deleted. Also search across them. |
|  | Edit records | `records:edit` | Create, edit, delete and restore records, and upload files. |
|  | Read comments | `records.comments:read` | View comments and replies on records. |
|  | Edit comments | `records.comments:edit` | Post comments and replies, and delete your own. |
|  | Share records | `records:share` | Change who can see and edit individual records. This gives other people access. |
| **Automations** | Read automations | `automations:read` | View automations, their run history and their setup, including credentials for connected systems. |
|  | Edit automations | `automations:edit` | Create, edit, activate, deactivate and delete automations. Deactivating one stops the processes that depend on it. |
|  | Run automations | `automations:run` | Trigger and simulate automations on your behalf. An automation runs with the rights of the person who owns it, so it can do things the credential cannot, including in apps outside a token's content access. |
| **Advanced** | Manage webhooks | `webhooks:manage` | Create, list, verify and delete webhooks. A webhook keeps sending record, comment and app changes to an address you choose until someone deletes it, including after the credential that created it is revoked. |
|  | Send email | `email:send` | Send email on your behalf, using your organization's email settings. Without your own SMTP server, Tape sends from its own address. |

## Four rules worth knowing

**Editing doesn't include reading.** `records:edit` lets a credential write records, but not read them back. A write-only integration, such as an inbound sync, needs no read access. Grant both when you need both.

**Deleting is part of editing.** There's no separate delete capability. `records:edit` covers creating, changing, deleting and restoring records. `workspaces:edit` covers deleting a workspace and everything inside it.

**Identifying yourself needs nothing.** [`GET /v1/user`](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/user#retrieve-the-current-user) tells you which user a credential belongs to and requires no capability. It returns no other user.

**Search is filtered, not blocked.** [`/v1/search`](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/search) returns app and record results. It accepts a credential that holds *either* `apps:read` *or* `records:read`, and returns only the result types the credential may see. A credential with only `records:read` gets record results and no app results.

## Requesting scopes with OAuth

A personal access token gets its capabilities from the checkboxes in the settings. An OAuth app requests them in the `scope` parameter of its [authorization request](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/authorization-flow#2-send-the-user-to-tape):

```text
scope=apps:read records:read records:edit
```

### General behavior

-   **Separate scopes with a single space** (`%20` in a URL). Tabs, line breaks and other whitespace make the value unknown. Use the scope strings from the table above.
-   **Omitting `scope` grants the read tier**, `apps:read records:read`. So does a `scope` that's empty once Tape removes ignored values.
-   **Tape ignores OpenID Connect values.** It drops `openid`, `profile`, `email`, `address`, `phone` and `offline_access` without an error, because many client libraries send them unasked. Tape isn't an OpenID provider, and it issues a refresh token without `offline_access`.
-   **Any other unknown value fails the request** with `invalid_scope`.
-   **The user approves all requested scopes or none.** The consent screen lists the requested scopes one per line, so sending email, managing webhooks and inviting organization members each get their own line. An MCP client that requests exactly the scopes the Tape MCP server advertises sees a short fixed summary instead.
-   **Read `scope` in the token response** instead of assuming Tape granted your request as sent. It names exactly what the access token holds.

Request every scope your app needs in the first authorization. Scopes are fixed once the user approves. To add one later, the user has to approve again; see [Insufficient capabilities](#insufficient-capabilities).

## Insufficient capabilities

A credential that authenticates but lacks a capability the endpoint requires gets a `403`. The message names the kind of credential:

*Response*

```json
{
  "status_code": 403,
  "endpoint": "/v1/record/1",
  "error_code": "forbidden",
  "error_message": "This personal access token is missing the required scope(s): records:edit."
}
```

For an OAuth access token, the message reads `This OAuth access token is missing the required scope(s): records:edit.` Some endpoints accept any one of several capabilities, such as [`/v1/search`](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/search). They refuse a credential that holds none of them with a message that lists them all.

The response also carries a standard `WWW-Authenticate` header that names what the endpoint needs:

```http
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", error_description="This personal access token is missing the required scope(s): records:edit.", scope="records:edit"
```

The `scope` value lists what the *endpoint requires*, not what your credential holds. Among `403` responses, only a capability refusal carries this header. See [`403` and `404` mean different things](#403-and-404-mean-different-things).

> A refused request still costs credits
> 
> Tape checks capabilities after rate limiting, so a `403` uses rate limit credits like any other request. Retrying a call your credential can't make uses up your budget without ever succeeding.

### Fix a missing capability

-   **Personal access token.** A token's capabilities are fixed when you create it. You can only change its name afterwards. Create a new token with the capabilities your integration needs, switch to it, and revoke the old one.
-   **OAuth access token.** Send the user through a new [authorization request](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/authorization-flow) whose `scope` names the scopes the app already holds *plus* the missing one (*step-up authorization*). Approval creates a new connection with exactly those scopes. Revoke the earlier connection's refresh token once you've stored the new tokens; see [Asking for more scopes](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/authorization-flow#asking-for-more-scopes). The [Tape MCP server](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/mcp/overview) answers a missing scope with a `403` whose `scope` already names the full set.

### `403` and `404` mean different things

A request passes through independent checks. The status code and the `WWW-Authenticate` header together tell you which check refused it:

| Status | Meaning | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `403` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope"` and a `scope` value | The credential lacks a *capability* the endpoint requires | Create a token with that capability, or ask the user to approve it |
| `403` without that header | The user's own role or permissions in Tape do not allow this operation, for example changing a [view](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/view) needs share access (**Can share** or **Full access**) to its app. `error_message` says why | Change the user's access in Tape. A new token or a new approval doesn't help |
| `404` | The resource does not exist, the user cannot see it, or, for a personal access token, it is outside the token's [content access](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/personal-access-tokens#content-selection) | Check the user's access; for a token, create one that selects that workspace or app |

A `404` deliberately looks the same as a resource that doesn't exist, so it carries no `WWW-Authenticate` header. If a personal access token gets a `404` for a record or app you know exists, check the token's content access first. An OAuth access token has no content access, so a `404` is about the user's own access.

A missing permission on a record or app usually returns `400` with `record_no_permission` or `app_no_permission`, not `403`. See [Errors](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/errors).

## Endpoints unavailable to tokens

A few internal endpoints refuse personal access tokens and OAuth access tokens, whatever capabilities they hold. They're not part of the public API. Requests to them return a `403` with this message:

```text
This endpoint cannot be accessed with a personal access token.
```

For an OAuth access token, the message is `This endpoint cannot be accessed with an OAuth access token.`

Every endpoint in this reference is reachable with the right capability.

# Date & timezone

> Read, write and filter dates and datetimes in the Tape API, in your timezone or in UTC.

Read, write and filter dates and datetimes in the Tape API, in your timezone or in UTC.

Every temporal value in the Tape API is a *string*, never an epoch number or an object.

## Formats

| Format | Shape | Example | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Datetime | `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss` | `2021-03-04 05:30:00` | A point in time. |
| Date | `YYYY-MM-DD` | `2021-03-04` | The date part of a value; a calendar day. |
| Time | `HH:mm:ss` | `05:30:00` | The time-of-day part of a value. |

The datetime format is close to ISO 8601, but not identical:

```text
2021-03-04 05:30:00     ← Tape
2021-03-04T05:30:00Z    ← the equivalent in standardized ISO 8601
```

A space replaces the `T` separator. There's *no `Z` suffix, no numeric offset, and no fractional seconds*, so the property name, not the string, tells you the zone.

> Do responses include seconds?
> 
> Datetime properties in responses include `:ss`, also when it's `00`: `2021-03-04 05:30:00`, never `2021-03-04 05:30`. Seconds are optional in *request* bodies, but don't expect the shorter form back.
> 
> The exception is the pre-formatted `value` / `value_string` of a [calculation field value](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/field-value/calculation). It's a display string *without* seconds (`YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm`, or `YYYY-MM-DD` for a whole day).

## Local and UTC are returned side by side

The API returns *every* temporal property twice, with the same rule everywhere:

-   The *unsuffixed* property (`start`, `created_on`, `due_at`, `logged_at`) is the value in the *acting user's timezone*. Use it for display.
-   The `_utc` property (`start_utc`, `created_on_utc`, `due_at_utc`, `logged_at_utc`) is the same instant in *UTC*. Use it to compare, sort, store and calculate.

Only [two places](#the-two-exceptions) break this rule.

Field values give each half at three levels of detail: the full datetime, the date part and the time part. A date field value carries six properties per date:

| Property | Timezone | Format | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `start` | acting user | `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss` | `2021-03-03 22:30:00` |
| `start_date` | acting user | `YYYY-MM-DD` | `2021-03-03` |
| `start_time` | acting user | `HH:mm:ss` | `22:30:00` |
| `start_utc` | UTC | `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss` | `2021-03-04 05:30:00` |
| `start_date_utc` | UTC | `YYYY-MM-DD` | `2021-03-04` |
| `start_time_utc` | UTC | `HH:mm:ss` | `05:30:00` |

A `range_date` field value repeats all six with an `end` prefix: `end`, `end_date`, `end_time`, `end_utc`, `end_date_utc`, `end_time_utc`. Single-instant properties elsewhere in the API come as a pair: `created_on` / `created_on_utc`, `completed_at` / `completed_at_utc`, and so on.

> The two halves can disagree on the calendar day
> 
> The example above is one instant, `2021-03-04 05:30:00` UTC, read by a user in `America/Phoenix` (UTC-7). The local half falls on *March 3rd*, the UTC half on *March 4th*. Grouping by `start_date` and by `start_date_utc` gives different groups.

> Which values should an integration read?
> 
> Read `_utc` and convert to your own display timezone. The unsuffixed values depend on whose credential is in use, so they're a poor fit for anything cached, compared or stored. Daylight saving shows why: the local half of a stored instant shifts by an hour twice a year, while its `_utc` half never moves.

### Where "local" comes from

The timezone comes from the *timezone setting of the user who owns the credential*. It's not part of the request:

-   There's *no header, query parameter or body property* that sets the timezone on `/v1/*` routes.
-   Two credentials of two users with different timezone settings return *different* unsuffixed values for the same record. The `_utc` values are identical.
-   For an [automation API key](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/authentication#automation-api-key), Tape uses the automation's timezone.

No endpoint reports the timezone. To find the offset your credential uses, *compare the two halves of any timestamp*, for example `created_on` and `created_on_utc` on any record.

### Example

One record, read with two credentials: one owned by a user set to `America/Phoenix`, one by a user set to `Europe/Amsterdam`.

*Phoenix (UTC-7)*

```json
{
  "record_id": 1,
  "created_on": "2021-03-03 22:30:00",
  "created_on_utc": "2021-03-04 05:30:00",
  "fields": [
    {
      "field_id": 2,
      "external_id": "event_date",
      "type": "date",
      "field_type": "single_date",
      "values": [
        {
          "start": "2021-03-03 22:30:00",
          "start_date": "2021-03-03",
          "start_time": "22:30:00",
          "start_utc": "2021-03-04 05:30:00",
          "start_date_utc": "2021-03-04",
          "start_time_utc": "05:30:00"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

*Amsterdam (UTC+1)*

```json
{
  "record_id": 1,
  "created_on": "2021-03-04 06:30:00",
  "created_on_utc": "2021-03-04 05:30:00",
  "fields": [
    {
      "field_id": 2,
      "external_id": "event_date",
      "type": "date",
      "field_type": "single_date",
      "values": [
        {
          "start": "2021-03-04 06:30:00",
          "start_date": "2021-03-04",
          "start_time": "06:30:00",
          "start_utc": "2021-03-04 05:30:00",
          "start_date_utc": "2021-03-04",
          "start_time_utc": "05:30:00"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

### The two exceptions

Two places don't return a local and a UTC value side by side. Both are deliberate.

| Where | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| [Calculation field value](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/field-value/calculation): `value`, `value_string` | Pre-formatted *display strings*, built from the local `start_date` / `start_time` and rendered without seconds. They have *no `_utc` sibling*. To compare or store a calculation date result, read `start_utc` from the same value object rather than parsing `value`. |
| [Automation usage report](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/automation-usage-report): `from`, `to` | Edges of the reporting intervals that had activity in the bucket, not event timestamps and not the edges of the calendar bucket. The `_utc` siblings exist so the API is uniform, but *all four values are UTC*. |

### A note on `_on` versus `_at`

Property names use two suffixes for the same concept: `created_on` in some places, `created_at` in others. The split is historical, not meaningful.

-   **`_on`:** the earliest resources, such as records, comments, replies, revisions, files, organizations, and attachment and image previews.
-   **`_at`:** resources and values added later, such as automations and runs, checklist entries, calculation script config, and the authorship metadata on email, phone and link values.

Both use the same formats and meaning, and both have a `_utc` sibling.

## Calendar days

A date field value holds either a *point in time* or a *whole calendar day* without a time. The API has no `all_day` flag. Two signals mark a calendar day:

1.  **`start_time` and `start_time_utc` are `null`.**
2.  **The local and UTC halves are identical.** Tape doesn't convert a calendar day between timezones: March 4th is March 4th for every user, in every zone.

*A whole day — 2021-03-04*

```json
{
  "start": "2021-03-04 00:00:00",
  "start_date": "2021-03-04",
  "start_time": null,
  "start_utc": "2021-03-04 00:00:00",
  "start_date_utc": "2021-03-04",
  "start_time_utc": null
}
```

*A point in time — 2021-03-04 at midnight UTC, read in Amsterdam*

```json
{
  "start": "2021-03-04 01:00:00",
  "start_date": "2021-03-04",
  "start_time": "01:00:00",
  "start_utc": "2021-03-04 00:00:00",
  "start_date_utc": "2021-03-04",
  "start_time_utc": "00:00:00"
}
```

> `start` is a midnight timestamp even for a whole day
> 
> A calendar day still returns `start` and `start_utc` as a full `YYYY-MM-DD 00:00:00` datetime. From `start` alone, you can't tell a whole day from a real midnight timestamp, as the second example shows. Test `start_time === null`, or read the date-only `start_date`.

A `range_date` value of whole days follows the same rule on both ends: `start_time` and `end_time` are both `null`, and every local property equals its `_utc` twin. A range can't mix a whole-day start with a timed end. Both ends are the same kind.

Checklist entry due dates use the same convention on `due_at_time` / `due_at_time_utc`.

## Writing field values

Requests accept the same three formats:

| Input | Interpreted as |
| --- | --- |
| `"2021-03-04"` | A whole calendar day. |
| `"2021-03-04 05:30"` | A point in time. Seconds may be omitted. |
| `"2021-03-04 05:30:00"` | A point in time. |
| `"2021-03-04 - 2021-03-06"` | A range. Split on a hyphen surrounded by single spaces. |

> Field values you write are read as UTC, not as your timezone
> 
> By default, Tape stores a datetime you send as UTC. Send `"2021-03-04 05:30:00"` as a user in `Europe/Amsterdam`, and the record reads back as `06:30:00` in `start` and `05:30:00` in `start_utc`. [Date filters](#filtering-by-date), by contrast, are read in your timezone.

Convert to UTC before sending, or add the query parameter `apply_user_timezone_on_date_inputs=true` to the record [create](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/record#create-a-record) and [update](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/record#update-a-record) endpoints (single and batch). Tape then reads a datetime without an offset in the calling user's timezone.

The parameter applies to date, date range and checklist due date values. `start_utc`, `end_utc` and `due_at_utc` properties, and values that state their own offset, aren't shifted.

The field's `time` setting also decides whether a written value becomes a calendar day or a timestamp. See [Date field](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/field/date).

| `settings.time` | Effect on a written value |
| --- | --- |
| `disabled` | Stored as a calendar day. Tape discards any time component you send. |
| `enabled` | A bare `YYYY-MM-DD` is stored as a calendar day; anything with a time as a timestamp. |
| `required` | Stored as a timestamp. A bare `YYYY-MM-DD` becomes midnight UTC. |

Field values also accept an object form. A `_utc` property in it takes precedence over its unsuffixed counterpart, so you can write a value read from the API straight back unchanged. See [Date field value](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/field-value/date) for the accepted object shapes.

## Filtering by date

Endpoints that accept a date window take each bound in *both* forms. [Search](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/search) accepts all eight parameters below. The general [automation run](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/automation-run) listing accepts the four `created_at_*` bounds only.

| Parameter | Read as |
| --- | --- |
| `created_at_from` | Your timezone |
| `created_at_from_utc` | UTC |
| `created_at_to` | Your timezone |
| `created_at_to_utc` | UTC |
| `last_modified_at_from` | Your timezone |
| `last_modified_at_from_utc` | UTC |
| `last_modified_at_to` | Your timezone |
| `last_modified_at_to_utc` | UTC |

### General behavior

-   All bounds use `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss` and are inclusive.
-   Each bound is independent. Send only a `_from` for "since", only a `_to` for "until", or both for a closed window.
-   A `_from` later than its matching `_to` returns `400`.
-   Tape reads the unsuffixed form in the same timezone it uses for `created_on`. A value taken from a result means the same instant when you send it back as a bound.
-   If you send both forms of the same bound, the `_utc` one wins.

> Polling for changes?
> 
> Use the `_utc` bounds: a wall-clock time carries no offset, so it's ambiguous when daylight saving ends and the same local hour occurs twice. Pass `last_modified_at_from_utc` with the `last_modified_on_utc` of your last result. The loop then never reads a window twice or skips one.

## Automations

Automations use the same paired local and UTC variables. Scripts run in UTC, so convert a local time before you write it. See [Date, time & timezones](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/automations/date-timezone).

# Errors

> Use the HTTP status and the error_code of a response to find out why a request failed.

Use the HTTP status and the `error_code` of a response to find out why a request failed.

This is the response for a record that doesn't exist:

```json
{
  "status_code": 404,
  "endpoint": "/v1/record/123",
  "error_code": "record_not_exists",
  "error_message": "Record does not exist(123)!"
}
```

The HTTP status gives the class of the error. The response body adds detail in `error_code` and `error_message`.

## Error codes

| Status | error\_code | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | `validation` | The request is not valid: the body is not valid JSON, doesn't match the expected parameters, or the credential is invalid, malformed or can't be used for this endpoint. Check the `error_message` property for details. |
| 400 | `input_validation` | The body doesn't match the endpoint's schema. `error_message` starts with `Invalid input:` and names each property that fails, for example `data/name must NOT have fewer than 1 characters`. |
| 400 | `bad_request` | The request is malformed, for example an empty `records` array in a batch request. |
| 400 | `record_no_permission` / `app_no_permission` | The user has no permission for this record or app. |
| 400 | `record_deleted` | The record is in the trash. |
| 400 | `workspace_invalid_permission` | The user has no permission for this workspace, for example no **Admin** role in it. |
| 400 | `deletions_rejected` | The request was sent with `reject_deletions=true` and would delete a field or an option. Tape applies nothing from the request. See [Update an app](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/app#update-an-app). |
| 401 | `dev_api_authentication` | The request carries no personal access token, OAuth access token or user API key. |
| 401 | `unauthorized` | The credential type isn't accepted for this endpoint (for example an automation API key on an endpoint that needs a credential acting for a user), or the user may not perform this operation. `error_message` says why. |
| 401 | `dev_api_invalid_access_token` | The OAuth access token is expired, revoked or otherwise no longer valid. Refresh it, or connect again. See [OAuth errors](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/authorization-flow#at-the-developer-api). |
| 403 | `forbidden` | The request is not allowed. If the response carries `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope"`, the personal access token or OAuth access token lacks a [capability](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/capabilities) this endpoint requires. See [Insufficient capabilities](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/capabilities#insufficient-capabilities). Otherwise the operation was refused for another reason, such as the user's permissions; `error_message` says why. |
| 404 | `not_found` | The resource doesn't exist, isn't shared with the owner of the credential, or lies outside a personal access token's [content access](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/personal-access-tokens#content-selection). An unknown path, or a method a path doesn't support, also returns `not_found` (for example `Cannot GET /v1/recrods`). |
| 404 | `record_not_exists` | The requested record doesn't exist. |
| 404 | `app_not_exists` | The requested app doesn't exist. |
| 409 | `conflict` | The resource is in a state that doesn't allow this operation, for example activating or running a broken automation. |
| 429 | `user_too_many_requests` | This request exceeds the number of requests allowed. Wait the seconds in the `Retry-After` header, then retry. See [rate limits](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/request-limits#rate-limits). |
| 500 | `unknown` | An unexpected error occurred. Reach out to [Tape support](mailto:team@tapeapp.com). |

## General behavior

-   Endpoints can return other, more specific `error_code` values. Handle an unknown `error_code` by its HTTP status.
-   A missing permission on a record or app returns `400`, not `403`. Check `error_code` to tell it apart from other `400` errors.
-   A request body that isn't valid JSON returns `400` with `validation`. The message starts with "A valid JSON body is required for operation".

**Getting an error?**

**403 error**

Check the `WWW-Authenticate` header. With `insufficient_scope`, [fix the missing capability](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/capabilities#fix-a-missing-capability): create a new token, or ask the user of an OAuth app to approve it. Without that header, the user's own permissions in Tape refuse the request.

# Tape Developer API

> Use the Tape API to read and change records, apps and workspaces, and to connect other services to Tape.

Use the Tape API to read and change records, apps and workspaces, and to connect other services to Tape.

> New to the Tape API?
> 
> Start with the [Quickstart](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/guide/api/getting-started). It takes you to your first request in two steps.

## Conventions

Send every request to the base URL `https://api.tapeapp.com`. The API requires HTTPS.

The API follows RESTful conventions where possible. Most operations use `GET`, `POST`, `PUT` and `DELETE` requests. Request and response bodies are JSON.

### JSON conventions

-   Property names use snake\_case, not camelCase or kebab-case.
-   Dates and datetimes are strings in an ISO 8601-like format. A datetime includes the time (`2020-08-12 02:12:33`), a date only the date (`2020-08-12`). See [Date & timezone](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/date-timezone).

## Code samples

Every endpoint shows a sample request and response. Requests use cURL.

The samples use a [personal access token](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/personal-access-tokens), the recommended credential. Send it as a bearer token in the `Authorization` header, or with the cURL option `-u` (`-u tape_pat_…:`). A user API key works the same way.

Most samples read the token from the environment variable `TAPE_TOKEN` and use example IDs such as `1`. Replace them with your own.

-   [Quickstart](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/guide/api/getting-started): retrieve your first record.
-   [Coming from the Podio API](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/guide/api/coming-from-podio): move an existing integration to Tape.
-   [Tape API guide, first steps](https://community.tapeapp.com/t/tape-api-guide-first-steps/2522): try three requests in Postman, no code needed.
-   [Authentication](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/authentication): choose between personal access tokens, user API keys and OAuth.
-   [Capabilities](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/capabilities): what each endpoint requires.
-   [Errors](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/errors): status codes and error codes.
-   [Request limits](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/request-limits): stay within the request budget.
-   [Pagination](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/pagination): page through long lists.
-   In the Help Center: [Tape API](https://help.tapeapp.com/en/articles/18449283-tape-api)
-   In the Help Center: [Intro to Tape for developers](https://help.tapeapp.com/en/articles/6448126-intro-to-tape-for-developers)

# The OAuth authorization flow

> Connect a user's Tape account step by step. PKCE, the authorization request, consent, the code exchange, refreshing, step-up, disconnecting, and errors.

Use this flow to connect one user's Tape account to your app.

Tape supports one flow: the authorization code flow with PKCE. You need a [client ID](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/clients) first.

Most OAuth client libraries implement every step below. Point yours at Tape's [metadata document](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/overview#endpoints), and it finds the endpoints itself.

## Step 1: Create a code verifier and challenge

Create a fresh random *code verifier* for every authorization. Derive its *code challenge* from it: `BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier))`, without padding. Keep the verifier on your side until the code exchange, in your backend session or in the app's memory.

```shell
code_verifier=$(openssl rand -base64 48 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=\n')
code_challenge=$(printf '%s' "$code_verifier" | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl base64 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=\n')
```

The verifier must be 43 to 128 characters from `A–Z`, `a–z`, `0–9` and `-._~`. The challenge has 43 characters.

## Step 2: Send the user to Tape

Redirect the user's browser to the authorization endpoint:

```text
https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/authorize
  ?response_type=code
  &client_id=tape_oc_8f14e45fceea167a5a36dedd4bea2543
  &redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2Foauth%2Fcallback
  &scope=apps%3Aread%20records%3Aread%20records%3Aedit
  &state=af0ifjsldkj
  &code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM
  &code_challenge_method=S256
```

| Parameter | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `response_type` | Yes | `code`. |
| `client_id` | Yes | Your client ID. |
| `redirect_uri` | Yes | One of your registered [redirect URIs](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/clients#redirect-uris). Required even if you registered only one. |
| `code_challenge` | Yes | The challenge from step 1. |
| `code_challenge_method` | Recommended | `S256`. If omitted, Tape assumes `S256`. Tape refuses `plain`. |
| `state` | Recommended | An unguessable value bound to the user's browser session. Tape returns it unchanged. Check it on the way back to prevent CSRF. |
| `scope` | No | Space-separated [scopes](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/capabilities#requesting-scopes-with-oauth). Defaults to `apps:read records:read`. |
| `resource` | No | `https://api.tapeapp.com/v1` or `https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp`, and may repeat. Accepted for compatibility. The token works at both either way. |

Tape ignores other parameters, such as `nonce`.

## Step 3: Let the user approve

Tape asks the user to sign in if needed. The **Connect with Tape** consent screen then shows the organization to connect under **Select organization**, and:

-   Your app's name. For a [self-registered](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/clients#register-a-client-yourself) client, it shows the client ID URL or the redirect host instead. A client Tape can't tie to a website carries the badge **Unverified**: one with a custom URL scheme shows that scheme, one that returns to a loopback address shows its `software_id` or the `client_name` it registered with, in lowercase. For a self-registered client, the screen reads **Connect with Tape MCP**.
-   What your app can do, one line per scope you requested.

![Connect with Tape MCP consent screen for a self-registered client: the line Grant acme sales sync access to Tape with the badge Unverified, Select organization, the scopes, Continue and Cancel](https://developers.tapeapp.com/assets/images/consent-unverified-db1b2cac035d369597fe147b326b9016.png)

The user approves *all* the requested scopes with **Continue**, or declines with **Cancel**. An authorization request expires if the user doesn't decide in time.

> Why can't some users approve?
> 
> -   **Organization guests** can't connect apps.
> -   **An organization can restrict apps.** Owners and admins can allow only approved apps for new connections, or limit an app to owners and admins. The consent screen tells a blocked member why, and the member can ask an admin.

## Step 4: Handle the callback

Tape redirects the browser to your `redirect_uri`:

```text
https://app.example.com/oauth/callback
  ?code=tape_oac_4b227777d4dd1fc61c6f884f48641d02b4d121d3fd328cb08b5531fcacdabf8a
  &state=af0ifjsldkj
  &iss=https%3A%2F%2Fapi.tapeapp.com
```

Before you use the code, check two values:

-   `state` is the value you sent.
-   `iss` is `https://api.tapeapp.com`.

If the user declines, you receive `access_denied`:

```text
https://app.example.com/oauth/callback
  ?error=access_denied
  &state=af0ifjsldkj
  &iss=https%3A%2F%2Fapi.tapeapp.com
```

### General behavior

-   **An invalid request still reaches your app,** for example an unknown scope, a malformed PKCE challenge, or an unsupported `resource`. Tape asks the user to sign in, then shows an error page with the reason ID. When the user selects **Return to app**, your `redirect_uri` receives `error` (`invalid_request`, `invalid_scope`, `invalid_target` or `unsupported_response_type`) and an `error_description` that ends in the reason ID.
-   **An untrusted client gets no redirect.** When Tape can't trust the `client_id` or `redirect_uri` itself, because it is unknown, revoked, or not registered, the user sees an error page instead. A request that prefers `application/json` gets a `400` with an `invalid_client` body.

## Step 5: Exchange the code for tokens

Post the code to the token endpoint within 60 seconds:

*Confidential client*

```shell
curl https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token \
  -u "tape_oc_8f14e45fceea167a5a36dedd4bea2543:tape_ocs_..." \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code \
  -d code=tape_oac_4b2277... \
  -d code_verifier="$code_verifier" \
  -d redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/oauth/callback
```

*Public client*

```shell
curl https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token \
  -d client_id=tape_oc_8f14e45fceea167a5a36dedd4bea2543 \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code \
  -d code=tape_oac_4b2277... \
  -d code_verifier="$code_verifier" \
  -d redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/oauth/callback
```

`redirect_uri` is optional here. If you send it, it must equal the value from step 2 exactly.

*Response*

```json
{
  "access_token": "tape_oat_9a3f...",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "refresh_token": "tape_ort_3f9a...",
  "scope": "apps:read records:read records:edit",
  "tape_user_id": 45,
  "tape_organization_id": 7
}
```

**Key fields**

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `access_token` | Send it as `Authorization: Bearer` to the API. |
| `expires_in` | Seconds until the access token expires, at most 3600. |
| `refresh_token` | Gets new access tokens. Store it securely, on your server where you can. |
| `scope` | The scopes *this access token* holds. Read it instead of assuming Tape granted your request as sent. |
| `tape_user_id` | The connected Tape user. Key your accounts on it: a person who belongs to two Tape organizations is two Tape users. |
| `tape_organization_id` | The organization the user chose on the consent screen. |

> Never retry a code exchange
> 
> A code is single use: Tape treats a code presented twice as stolen, even your own retry after a timeout. It then *disconnects* the connection the code created and answers `invalid_grant`. If an exchange fails, start a new authorization instead.

## Step 6: Call the API

```shell
curl https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/user \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer tape_oat_9a3f..."
```

The token acts as the connected user, limited to the approved scopes. It works at the [Developer API](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/introduction) and the [Tape MCP server](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/mcp/overview) alike. [`GET /v1/user`](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/user#retrieve-the-current-user) needs no scope and reports the token's scopes in its response.

## Refreshing an access token

An access token lasts one hour. Get a new one with the refresh token:

```shell
curl https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token \
  -u "tape_oc_8f14e45fceea167a5a36dedd4bea2543:tape_ocs_..." \
  -d grant_type=refresh_token \
  -d refresh_token=tape_ort_3f9a...
```

A public client sends `-d client_id=tape_oc_...` instead of `-u`, here and when [disconnecting](#disconnecting).

What happens to the refresh token depends on your client type:

-   **Public clients rotate.** Every refresh returns a new refresh token and uses up the one you sent, so store the new one every time. Re-sending a used refresh token within 30 seconds, for example as a retry after a timeout, returns a fresh pair, up to three times. Tape treats a later re-send, or a fourth one, as theft: it disconnects the connection for every device that holds it, and the user has to connect again.
-   **Confidential clients keep theirs.** The refresh token from the code exchange stays valid for the life of the connection. A refresh returns only a new access token, without `refresh_token`. Concurrent refreshes are fine.

Send `scope` to get an access token with *fewer* scopes than the connection holds. `scope` never adds scopes. A `scope` outside the connection fails with `invalid_scope` and leaves the refresh token usable.

### General behavior

-   Every refresh keeps the connection alive. A connection that gets no new token for 90 days expires.
-   A connection also ends 365 days after the user approved it, however active it is. This doesn't apply when Tape registered your client as a confidential one.
-   When a refresh fails with `invalid_grant`, the connection is gone. Send the user through the authorization flow again.

## Asking for more scopes

When your app calls an endpoint that needs a scope the token lacks, the API answers `403` with:

```http
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", error_description="This OAuth access token is missing the required scope(s): records:edit.", scope="records:edit"
```

To get the missing scope:

1.  Send the user through the authorization flow again.
2.  Set `scope` to the scopes you *already hold plus the missing one*. If you ask for the missing scope alone, you end up with only that scope.
3.  The user approves the new set. You get a new connection with exactly those scopes.
4.  Store the new tokens, then [revoke](#disconnecting) the old refresh token. The new approval doesn't end the earlier connection, so the user would otherwise keep an unused one.

Ask for everything you need up front, so you don't send the user back to the consent screen. See [Insufficient capabilities](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/capabilities#insufficient-capabilities).

## Disconnecting

To disconnect, revoke the *refresh token*:

```shell
curl https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/revoke \
  -u "tape_oc_8f14e45fceea167a5a36dedd4bea2543:tape_ocs_..." \
  -d token=tape_ort_3f9a... \
  -d token_type_hint=refresh_token
```

-   **A refresh token** ends the whole connection. Every access token issued for it stops working on the next request.
-   **An access token** revokes only that one access token. The connection keeps working.
-   Once your client authenticates and sends a `token`, the endpoint answers `200` with an empty body. This includes a token that is unknown, already revoked, or not your client's.

A connection also ends when:

-   the user disconnects your app in Tape, under **Preferences** → **Connections**, or an organization admin disconnects it for them or for everyone,
-   the user is deactivated or removed from the organization, or becomes a guest,
-   an organization admin blocks your app for the user, for example by restricting it to **Owners and admins**,
-   it expires, as described under [Refreshing](#refreshing-an-access-token).

Changing a password doesn't end connections.

### One connection per approval

Every approval creates its own connection, with its own tokens. Connecting the same app from a second device doesn't disconnect the first. A user can hold up to 10 connections to the same app, and an eleventh ends the oldest.

A client Tape registered to keep one connection per user is the exception. There, each new sign-in replaces the user's previous connection, so store the newest tokens every time.

## Errors

### At the OAuth endpoints

The token, revocation, and registration endpoints answer errors in the standard OAuth shape. `error_description` ends with a *reason ID* in brackets. Errors from the authorization endpoint carry the same reason IDs: in the redirect's `error_description`, on Tape's error page, or in a `400` JSON body.

```json
{
  "error": "invalid_grant",
  "error_description": "The authorization code is unknown or has expired. [TOKEN_CODE_UNKNOWN]"
}
```

Quote the reason ID when you contact Tape support. It names the exact cause.

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | In general. |
| `401` | With `invalid_client`, when client authentication fails. |
| `429` | With `temporarily_unavailable` and a `Retry-After` header, when you are rate limited. |

The reason IDs you are most likely to meet:

| Reason ID | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `AUTHORIZE_CLIENT_INVALID` | The `client_id` is missing, unknown or revoked. Tape removes a [dynamically registered](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/clients#dynamic-client-registration) client that no user connected within 25 hours, and it lands here. Register again. |
| `AUTHORIZE_REDIRECT_URI_INVALID` | `redirect_uri` is missing or matches no registered URI. |
| `AUTHORIZE_CIMD_DOCUMENT_INVALID` | Tape couldn't fetch your [client ID metadata document](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/clients#client-id-metadata-document), or it is invalid. |
| `AUTHORIZE_PKCE_INVALID` | No code challenge, a method other than `S256`, or a malformed challenge. |
| `AUTHORIZE_SCOPE_UNKNOWN` | A requested scope doesn't exist. Check for typos, and separate scopes with single spaces. |
| `AUTHORIZE_RESOURCE_INVALID` | `resource` is neither `https://api.tapeapp.com/v1` nor `https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp`. |
| `CLIENT_AUTH_FAILED` | Unknown client, wrong or missing secret, or a public client sending a secret. |
| `CLIENT_AUTH_AMBIGUOUS` | More than one client authentication method in one request. |
| `TOKEN_CODE_UNKNOWN` | The code expired (after 60 seconds) or was never issued. |
| `TOKEN_CODE_REPLAYED` | The code was used before. Tape disconnected its connection. |
| `TOKEN_CODE_BINDING_MISMATCH` | The code belongs to another client, or `redirect_uri` differs from the authorization request. |
| `TOKEN_PKCE_VERIFIER_PRESENCE` / `TOKEN_PKCE_VERIFIER_MISMATCH` | `code_verifier` is missing, or doesn't match the challenge. |
| `TOKEN_CODE_REDEMPTION_REFUSED` | The user can no longer connect your app: deactivated, a guest, or blocked by the organization's app settings. |
| `TOKEN_REFRESH_TOKEN_UNKNOWN` | Not a refresh token of this client. |
| `TOKEN_REFRESH_GRANT_INACTIVE` | The connection was disconnected or expired, or the organization now blocks your app. Start a new authorization. |
| `TOKEN_REFRESH_SCOPE_INVALID` | The refresh asked for a scope the connection doesn't hold. Nothing was used up. |
| `TOKEN_REFRESH_REPLAYED` | A public client re-sent a used refresh token too late or too often. Tape disconnected the connection. |

### At the developer API

The API answers in its own [error format](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/errors). An access token that is no longer valid gets the same `401`, whatever the cause: expired, revoked, disconnected, or blocked by the organization.

```json
{
  "status_code": 401,
  "endpoint": "/v1/record/1",
  "error_code": "dev_api_invalid_access_token",
  "error_message": "Invalid access token for accessing endpoint '/v1/record/1' (the access token is not active)"
}
```

```http
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://api.tapeapp.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/v1", error="invalid_token", error_description="The access token is not active."
```

Refresh the access token. If the refresh fails with `invalid_grant`, start a new authorization. A missing scope is a `403`, covered under [Asking for more scopes](#asking-for-more-scopes).

## Differences from the specifications

Tape follows OAuth 2.1 and the related RFCs, with these deliberate differences:

-   **One token for both Tape resources.** Every access token is valid at the Developer API and the MCP server, whichever `resource` you asked for.
-   **`redirect_uri` is required** in every authorization request, even with a single registered redirect URI.
-   **A missing `code_challenge_method` means `S256`**, not `plain`.
-   **Revoking another client's token answers `200`** and revokes nothing. Nobody can use the endpoint to find out whose token it is.
-   **Tape doesn't support `private_key_jwt`.** Tape accepts a client ID metadata document that prefers it as a public client, if the document also lists `none`. Tape ignores `jwks_uri`.
-   **Tape can waive PKCE** for a confidential client it registered, on request. A code issued without PKCE requires `redirect_uri` at the token endpoint.

# Register an OAuth client

> Get an OAuth client ID for Tape. Registered by Tape for integrations, or self-registered through a client ID metadata document or dynamic client registration.

Get the client ID that every [OAuth](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/overview) app needs.

There are three ways to get a client ID:

| How | Best for | Client secret | On the consent screen |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Registered by Tape](#a-client-registered-by-tape) | Integrations and partner products | Optional | Your app's name |
| [Client ID metadata document](#client-id-metadata-document) | MCP clients and AI platforms | None, public client | Its client ID URL, or its name if Tape recognizes it |
| [Dynamic client registration](#dynamic-client-registration) | MCP clients that support it | None, public client | Its redirect host, or the badge **Unverified** |

Do you only call the API from your own code? You need no client at all. Use a [personal access token](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/personal-access-tokens).

## A client registered by Tape

Email [team@tapeapp.com](mailto:team@tapeapp.com) with:

-   your app's *name*, a short description, and its website,
-   its *redirect URIs*: the exact URLs Tape may send the user back to (see [Redirect URIs](#redirect-uris)),
-   whether it has a *backend* that can keep a secret (a *confidential* client), or runs entirely on the user's device or in a browser (a *public* client),
-   for a confidential client, whether your app keeps *one* connection per Tape user. With that setting, a new sign-in replaces the user's previous connection. This is usual for a "Sign in with Tape" backend. See the [integration guide](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/sign-in-with-tape).

You receive a client ID that starts with `tape_oc_`. A confidential client also gets a client secret that starts with `tape_ocs_`.

> Tape shares the secret only once
> 
> Store the client secret in your backend's secret store. Never ship it in a browser, mobile, or desktop app.

### General behavior

-   The consent screen shows a client registered by Tape under your app's name.
-   A confidential client's connections never reach an absolute expiry. An unattended sync keeps running as long as it refreshes at least once every 90 days.

> Rotating the client secret?
> 
> When Tape rotates your client secret, the previous secret keeps working for a transition period: seven days, unless agreed otherwise. Deploy the new secret before the old one stops.

## Register a client yourself

An MCP client or AI platform can't be registered by hand for every server it talks to. Self-registration lets it connect to the [Tape MCP server](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/mcp/overview) without anyone setting it up first. Tape supports the two standard ways to do this.

Both create a *public* client. A public client has no secret and proves possession with [PKCE](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/authorization-flow#1-create-a-pkce-verifier-and-challenge) alone.

Tape treats a client that registers itself as an MCP client:

-   Its consent screen reads **Connect with Tape MCP**.
-   Organization owners and admins manage it under **Tape MCP** in their settings.

![Consent screen titled Connect with Tape MCP for a self-registered client, with Select organization, the scopes, Continue and Cancel](https://developers.tapeapp.com/assets/images/consent-tape-mcp-daf71db289716b866f258dc1c3f7fc7e.png)

### Client ID metadata document

With a client ID metadata document, the client ID *is* an `https` URL. That URL serves a JSON document that describes the client. Tape fetches the document the first time a user starts a sign-in, so there is no registration request at all.

*https://app.example.com/oauth/client-metadata.json*

```json
{
  "client_id": "https://app.example.com/oauth/client-metadata.json",
  "client_name": "Example Assistant",
  "client_uri": "https://app.example.com",
  "redirect_uris": ["https://app.example.com/oauth/callback", "http://127.0.0.1/callback"],
  "grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
  "response_types": ["code"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none"
}
```

#### Requirements

**The URL** must:

-   use `https` and have a path,
-   contain no credentials or fragment,
-   be in canonical form and at most 2048 characters long,
-   have a domain name as its host, not an IP address, and name no port.

**The document** must:

-   name the URL itself as its `client_id`,
-   list at least one `redirect_uris` entry, each one [admissible](#redirect-uris),
-   be a public client: `token_endpoint_auth_method` is `none`, or `none` appears in `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported`,
-   include `authorization_code` in `grant_types`, if `grant_types` is present.

Tape ignores members it doesn't use.

#### How Tape fetches the document

-   Tape requests the document on port 443, follows no redirects, and waits at most 5 seconds.
-   The response must be `200 OK` with `Content-Type: application/json`, uncompressed, and at most 5 KB.
-   Tape caches a document for up to an hour, so a change can take that long to apply.

Your host is unreachable, times out, answers `5xx`, `408` or `429`, or returns something that isn't a JSON document of at most 5 KB? Tape keeps using the last good copy for up to a day.

Your host answers any other `4xx`, a redirect, or a document that breaks the rules above? Tape discards its copy. Sign-ins stop until the host serves a valid document again.

#### On the consent screen

The consent screen shows the app by its client ID URL, or by its own name if Tape recognizes it. Tape doesn't mark it **Unverified**, because the document's address shows who published it. The document's `client_name` doesn't appear.

### Dynamic client registration

A client can also register by posting its metadata to the registration endpoint. No authentication is needed.

```shell
curl https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/register \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "client_name": "Example Assistant",
    "redirect_uris": ["http://127.0.0.1/callback"]
  }'
```

*Response (201 Created)*

```json
{
  "client_id": "tape_oc_8f14e45fceea167a5a36dedd4bea2543",
  "client_id_issued_at": 1791000000,
  "client_name": "Example Assistant",
  "redirect_uris": ["http://127.0.0.1/callback"],
  "grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
  "response_types": ["code"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none"
}
```

The response echoes what Tape *accepted*. It can differ from what you sent:

-   **Public clients only.** Tape issues no client secret and replaces any `token_endpoint_auth_method` with `none`.
-   **Redirect URIs are filtered.** Tape drops inadmissible entries and echoes the rest. The request fails with `invalid_redirect_uri` only when none remain. Send at most 10 entries and 4096 characters in total.
-   **`client_name`** is cut to 100 characters and defaults to the first redirect URI's host. Tape ignores `logo_uri`. It keeps `client_uri` only when it is an `https` URL, without credentials, on the host of one of your `https` redirect URIs.
-   **`scope` and `grant_types` never limit the client.** You choose scopes per authorization request, and Tape issues a refresh token either way. Tape drops unsupported `grant_types` values.

The request fails with `invalid_client_metadata` when:

-   `grant_types` is present without `authorization_code`,
-   `response_types` is anything other than `["code"]`,
-   the redirect URIs exceed the limits above.

#### General behavior

-   **Registration is idempotent for 24 hours.** Posting identical metadata again returns the same client ID. Every installation that registers with the same metadata shares one client ID, so treat it as public.
-   **Unused registrations expire.** Tape deletes a client that no user connected within 25 hours of registering, and eventually one whose connections have all ended. When the authorization endpoint then refuses your client ID with `AUTHORIZE_CLIENT_INVALID`, register again. A browser sees an error page, and a request that sends `Accept: application/json` gets a `400` with an `invalid_client` body.
-   **On the consent screen,** a client whose redirect URIs are all `https` on one host appears under that host. Any other self-registered client, one that returns to a loopback address or a custom URL scheme, carries the badge **Unverified**.

## Where Tape may redirect

The same rules apply to every kind of client. A redirect URI may be:

| Kind | Example | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `https` | `https://app.example.com/oauth/callback` | The usual choice for a web app. |
| Loopback `http` | `http://127.0.0.1/callback` | Only on `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]` or `localhost`. *Any port matches*, so register it without one. |
| Private-use scheme | `com.example.app:/oauth/callback` | For desktop and mobile apps. Tape refuses `javascript`, `data`, `file`, `blob` and similar schemes. |

A redirect URI must contain no credentials and no fragment, be in canonical form, and be at most 2048 characters long. The authorization request's `redirect_uri` must match a registered one *exactly*, apart from a loopback URI's port.

## Client authentication

The token and revocation endpoints identify the client in one of three ways. Use exactly one per request.

| Method | For | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `client_secret_basic` | Confidential client | HTTP Basic authentication, with the client ID as the username and the secret as the password. |
| `client_secret_post` | Confidential client | `client_id` and `client_secret` in the form body. |
| `none` | Public client | `client_id` in the form body. PKCE proves possession. |

### General behavior

-   A confidential client may use either secret method, regardless of which one it registered.
-   Tape refuses a secret sent both ways, or a body `client_id` that differs from the Basic username, with `invalid_request`.
-   Tape treats a public client that sends Basic authentication with an empty password as `none`.

# OAuth

> Let other Tape users connect your app to their account with OAuth 2.1. When to use it, supported flows, endpoints, and what an access token can do.

Use OAuth to let other Tape users connect your app to their Tape account without copying a secret.

Tape is an OAuth 2.1 authorization server. An access token calls the [Developer API](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/introduction) and the [Tape MCP server](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/mcp/overview) as the user who approved your app.

## When to use OAuth

OAuth is mainly for *MCP clients* and for *integrations and partners registered by Tape*.

| You are building | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A script, internal tool or integration that calls the API directly, including on a user's behalf | A [personal access token](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/personal-access-tokens) |
| An MCP client or AI platform | OAuth, with a client that [registers itself](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/clients#register-a-client-yourself) |
| An integration or partner product with a "Connect to Tape" or "Sign in with Tape" button | OAuth, with a [client registered by Tape](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/clients#a-client-registered-by-tape). See the [integration guide](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/sign-in-with-tape) |

A personal access token can do everything an OAuth token can do, and more. It needs no client registration, no redirect, no consent screen and no refreshing. You can limit it to selected workspaces and apps. See [Which credential to use](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/authentication#which-credential-to-use).

## How it works

1.  Your app sends the user's browser to Tape's *authorization endpoint* and names the scopes it needs.
2.  The user signs in to Tape if needed and chooses the organization to connect. The *consent screen* shows your app's name and what your app can do.
3.  The user approves. Tape redirects the browser back to your app with a short-lived *authorization code*.
4.  Your app exchanges the code at the *token endpoint* for an *access token* and a *refresh token*.
5.  Your app calls the API with the access token. The access token lasts one hour. Use the refresh token to get a new one.

Each approval creates a *connection* between the user and your app. A connection keeps working until one of these happens:

-   The user, an organization admin, or your app disconnects it.
-   The user loses access to the organization.
-   90 days pass without a refresh.
-   365 days pass since the user approved it. This doesn't apply when Tape registered your client as a confidential one.

[The authorization flow](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/authorization-flow) walks through every step.

> Where do users see their connections?
> 
> In Tape, users select their profile picture, then select **Preferences** → **Connections**. MCP clients appear under **Tape MCP** instead. Organization owners and admins manage connections for everyone on the **Manage** tab of the same pages.

![Connections page in the settings window with the tabs Browse Connections and Manage](https://developers.tapeapp.com/assets/images/connections-settings-c03ee32c778cabd969ac188e67b18bc5.png)

## Supported flows

| Grant type | Supported |
| --- | --- |
| Authorization code with PKCE (`authorization_code`) | Yes, the only way to get a token |
| Refresh token (`refresh_token`) | Yes |
| Client credentials | No |
| Device authorization | No |
| Implicit, resource owner password | No, OAuth 2.1 removes both |

-   **PKCE is required**, with the `S256` method. Tape refuses `plain`.
-   **The response type is `code`**, and the response mode is `query`.
-   **Tape is not an OpenID Connect provider.** There is no `id_token` and no OpenID userinfo endpoint. The token response names the user (`tape_user_id`), and [`GET /v1/user`](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/resource/user#retrieve-the-current-user) returns the rest.
-   **Tokens are opaque.** They are not JWTs. Don't try to decode them.

## Endpoints

The issuer is `https://api.tapeapp.com`.

| Endpoint | URL |
| --- | --- |
| Authorization server metadata (RFC 8414) | `GET https://api.tapeapp.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` |
| Authorization | `GET https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/authorize` |
| Token | `POST https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token` |
| Revocation (RFC 7009) | `POST https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/revoke` |
| Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591) | `POST https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/register` |
| Protected resource metadata, Developer API | `GET https://api.tapeapp.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/v1` |
| Protected resource metadata, Tape MCP | `GET https://mcp.tapeapp.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp` |

The authorization server metadata also lists an introspection endpoint. Tape reserves it for its own services, and it refuses every other client.

Discover the endpoints from the metadata instead of hard-coding them:

*GET https://api.tapeapp.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server*

```json
{
  "issuer": "https://api.tapeapp.com",
  "authorization_endpoint": "https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/authorize",
  "token_endpoint": "https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/token",
  "revocation_endpoint": "https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/revoke",
  "introspection_endpoint": "https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/introspect",
  "registration_endpoint": "https://api.tapeapp.com/oauth/register",
  "scopes_supported": ["apps:read", "records:read"],
  "response_types_supported": ["code"],
  "response_modes_supported": ["query"],
  "grant_types_supported": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post", "none"],
  "revocation_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post", "none"],
  "introspection_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post"],
  "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"],
  "client_id_metadata_document_supported": true,
  "authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported": true,
  "service_documentation": "https://developers.tapeapp.com/oauth"
}
```

`scopes_supported` lists only the default read scopes. You can request every scope in [Capabilities](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/capabilities).

### General behavior

-   The token and revocation endpoints take `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` bodies. Registration takes `application/json`.
-   Send each parameter at most once. Only `resource` may repeat.
-   The token, revocation, and registration endpoints and all three metadata documents allow cross-origin requests. An app that runs in a browser can call them.

## What an access token can do

-   **It acts as the user.** Its access is the user's own permissions, narrowed by the scopes the user approved. Records it creates or changes show the user as the author.
-   **It reaches everything the user can.** Unlike a personal access token, you can't limit an OAuth access token to selected workspaces and apps.
-   **It works at the Developer API and the MCP server alike.** One token is valid at `https://api.tapeapp.com/v1` and at `https://mcp.tapeapp.com/mcp`.
-   **It shares the user's rate limit.** Every connected app draws from the same per-user budget as the user's personal access tokens. See [Request limits](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/request-limits).

Send it as a bearer token, the same way as a personal access token:

```shell
curl https://api.tapeapp.com/v1/user \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer tape_oat_0a1b2c3d..."
```

### Credential formats

Every OAuth credential has a recognizable prefix. The prefix is part of the value. Store and send each credential exactly as you received it.

| Credential | Prefix | Lifetime |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access token | `tape_oat_` | 1 hour |
| Refresh token | `tape_ort_` | Public client: single use, each refresh returns a new one. Confidential client: as long as its connection. See [Refreshing](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/authorization-flow#refreshing-an-access-token) |
| Authorization code | `tape_oac_` | 60 seconds, single use |
| Client ID | `tape_oc_` | None. A [metadata document](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/clients#client-id-metadata-document) client uses its URL instead |
| Client secret | `tape_ocs_` | Until Tape rotates it |

## Next steps

-   [Register a client](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/clients): get a `client_id`, and a secret if your app has a backend.
-   [Authorization flow](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/authorization-flow): send each request step by step, then refresh, ask for more scopes, and disconnect.
-   [Integration guide](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/oauth/sign-in-with-tape): connect your product's users to Tape from your backend.
-   [Capabilities](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/capabilities): every scope you can request.
-   [Personal access tokens](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/personal-access-tokens): call the API directly without a client.
-   [Request limits](https://developers.tapeapp.com/docs/api/request-limits): the per-user budget connected apps share.
-   In the Help Center: [Connect apps with OAuth 2.1](https://help.tapeapp.com/en/articles/18449279-connect-apps-with-oauth-2-1)
